column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Allah is pure (ṭayyib) and accepts only what is pure.
Allah has commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, for the Exalted said: ‘O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds’ [al-Muʾminūn 23:51],
and the Exalted said: ‘O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you’ [al-Baqarah 2:172].”

Then he mentioned a man who travels far, dishevelled and covered in dust, stretching his hands towards the sky: “O Lord! O Lord!”—“while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful and he has been nourished with the unlawful; so how can he be answered?” Reported by Muslim.

Ṭayyib (“pure”): holy, free of deficiencies and faults. Ashʿath (“dishevelled”): with unkempt hair. Aghbar (“covered in dust”): his colour changed by the length of his travel. “Stretching his hands”: raising them in supplication to Allah. Ghudhiya (“he has been nourished”):

his body has been fed from the unlawful. “So how can he be answered?”: from where could one with these qualities be answered? Maṭʿamuhu: his food. Mashrabuhu: his drink. Malbasuhu: his clothing. “And he has been nourished with the unlawful”: what nourishes his body and soul.
When charity comes from unlawful wealth, Allah does not accept it.
The command to make deeds sincerely for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Encouragement to spend from what is lawful and the prohibition of spending from what is unlawful,
and the permissibility of eating of the good things.
When a person eats what is pure, intending by it to gain strength for obedience and to sustain himself, he is rewarded for that.
The hadith explains the conditions of supplication and what prevents it [from being answered].
Among the causes of supplication being answered are eating what is lawful and avoiding what is unlawful.
It is recommended to raise the hands towards the sky when wishing to supplicate.
It is prescribed to persist in supplication, mentioning His lordship.
Eating good things was permitted in the laws of the nations before us.

This hadith teaches us that Allah, Glorified is He, is free of deficiencies and faults and described by the attributes of perfection, so one does not seek nearness to Him with charity from unlawful wealth, or wealth in which there is doubt, or with poor food; and that Allah has permitted the believers to eat of the good things,
just as He permitted it to the messengers, along with doing righteous deeds and thanking Allah for His blessings.

Then the Messenger ﷺ made clear that just as Allah loves spending from the good and the best, He loves only the pure among deeds. Then he mentioned something like an example to warn his nation against the unlawful, saying: a man travels far,

that is, in various acts of obedience such as Ḥajj, jihād and earning a living, his hair dishevelled and his colour dusty from the length of his travel, stretching his hands towards the sky in supplication to Allah, beseeching Him and humbling himself before Him;

and yet he is not answered, because his earnings are not pure, since his food and drink are unlawful. So let every believer beware of having this quality that prevents supplication [from being answered].
On this meaning it has been said:
If you perform Ḥajj with wealth whose source is unlawful, / you have not performed Ḥajj—the caravan has.
Allah accepts only what is righteous; / not everyone who performs Ḥajj to the House of Allah has an accepted Ḥajj.
Another poet:
Bad food from bitter earnings / blinds the heart with its disease and deafens it.
So how can a worshipper prosper whose bones / and flesh have grown on unlawful gain?
Another poet:
Remember the scrutiny of the reckoning, for / all that you committed will surely be counted and written.
The two angels did not forget it when you forgot it; / rather, they recorded it while you were heedless, at play.
